1.hook: The lightest and most abundant element: one proton and one electron.
1.meet: Water, the Sun, and every organic molecule.

2.hook: So unreactive it forms no stable compounds, and it stays liquid down to absolute zero at normal pressure.
2.meet: Party balloons, cooling the magnets in MRI scanners.

3.hook: The lightest metal: soft enough to cut with a knife, and it floats on water.
3.meet: Rechargeable batteries in phones and electric cars.

4.hook: Light, stiff and almost transparent to X-rays, but its dust is toxic.
4.meet: X-ray windows, aerospace parts, the James Webb Space Telescope’s mirrors.

5.hook: A hard, dark semi-metal that stars destroy rather than make.
5.meet: Heat-proof borosilicate glass, detergents, neodymium magnets.

6.hook: Bonds to itself in endless chains and rings: the backbone of all known life.
6.meet: Every living thing, pencil graphite, diamonds, fuels.

7.hook: Its two atoms share a triple bond so strong that nitrogen gas barely reacts.
7.meet: Most of the air, fertilisers, proteins and DNA.

8.hook: Pulls electrons from almost everything; it is what makes fire and rust happen.
8.meet: The air you breathe, water, and nearly half of Earth’s crust by mass.

9.hook: The most reactive element of all; it even reacts with some noble gases.

10.hook: A noble gas that glows red-orange when electricity runs through it.

11.hook: A soft metal that fizzes in water and can burst into flame.
11.meet: Table salt, baking soda, the yellow glow of old street lamps.

12.hook: A light metal that burns with a blinding white flame.
12.meet: Chlorophyll in every green leaf, lightweight alloys, flares.

13.hook: The most abundant metal in Earth’s crust, protected by an invisible oxide skin.
13.meet: Drink cans, foil, aircraft, window frames.

14.hook: A semiconductor: doping it with traces of other elements made the computer age.
14.meet: Computer chips, solar cells, sand and glass.

15.hook: Comes in white, red and black forms; the white form glows and catches fire in air.
15.meet: DNA’s backbone, bones and teeth, fertilisers, match strikers.

16.hook: A bright yellow solid with no smell of its own; its compounds give rotten eggs their stink.

17.hook: A poisonous yellow-green gas that becomes harmless when bound up as salt.
17.meet: Table salt, swimming pools, PVC plastic, disinfectants.

18.hook: Almost 1% of the air, and it reacts with practically nothing.
18.meet: Light bulbs, welding gas, double-glazed windows.

19.hook: So reactive it bursts into a lilac flame in water.
19.meet: Bananas, potash fertiliser, the electrical signals in your nerves.

20.hook: A soft metal whose compounds build bones, shells and whole mountains of limestone.
20.meet: Bones and teeth, milk, chalk, cement.

21.hook: A rare, light metal Mendeleev predicted before anyone had found it.
21.meet: Aluminium–scandium alloys in bike frames and aircraft parts.

22.hook: As strong as many steels but about 45% lighter, and it shrugs off corrosion.
22.meet: Hip implants, aircraft, white paint (titanium dioxide).

23.hook: A little of it makes steel tough and springy.
23.meet: Tool steels, large vanadium flow batteries.

24.hook: Takes a mirror polish and keeps steel from rusting.
24.meet: Chrome plating, stainless steel, the colour of rubies and emeralds.

25.hook: Essential for steelmaking, and for the step of photosynthesis that splits water.

26.hook: The most-used metal on Earth, with one of the most tightly bound nuclei of all, which is why fusion in stars stops paying off here.
26.meet: Steel, the haemoglobin in your blood, Earth’s core.

27.hook: A magnetic metal whose compounds give glass a deep blue.
27.meet: Lithium-ion battery cathodes, blue glass, vitamin B12.

29.hook: The second-best electrical conductor; its reddish colour turns green outdoors.
29.meet: Wiring, plumbing, the Statue of Liberty.

30.hook: Sacrifices itself to keep steel from rusting.
30.meet: Galvanised steel, brass, sunscreen, hundreds of enzymes.

31.meet: Blue and white LEDs, fast phone chips.

32.hook: A semiconductor that came before silicon in the first transistors.

33.hook: A notorious poison that is also a useful semiconductor ingredient.
33.meet: Gallium arsenide chips in phones and satellites.

34.hook: Conducts electricity better in light than in the dark.

35.hook: One of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature; it fumes red-brown.
35.meet: Flame retardants, water treatment, old photographic film.

36.hook: A noble gas whose orange light once defined the length of a metre.

37.hook: Melts just above body temperature and ignites on contact with air.

38.hook: Burns with a brilliant crimson flame.

39.hook: Named after Ytterby, a Swedish village that gave its name to four elements.

40.hook: Almost transparent to neutrons and very hard to corrode.
40.meet: Nuclear fuel cladding, cubic zirconia jewellery, ceramic knives.

41.hook: Becomes a superconductor at 9.2 K, the highest temperature of any element at normal pressure.
41.meet: MRI and particle-accelerator magnets, jet-engine alloys.

42.hook: Melts above 2,600 °C and makes steel stronger at high temperatures.
42.meet: High-strength steels; the enzymes bacteria use to fix nitrogen.

43.hook: The lightest element with no stable isotope, and the first ever made artificially.
43.meet: Medical imaging: tens of millions of scans a year.

44.hook: A hard, rare platinum-group metal that makes contacts last.
44.meet: Hard drives, electrical contacts, chemical catalysts.

45.hook: One of the rarest and most expensive metals.
45.meet: Catalytic converters, the bright finish on white-gold jewellery.

46.hook: Soaks up hundreds of times its own volume of hydrogen.

47.hook: Conducts electricity and heat better than any other metal.

48.hook: A toxic metal once common in rechargeable batteries.
48.meet: Nickel–cadmium batteries, bright yellow and red pigments.

49.hook: So soft you can scratch it with a fingernail, and it sticks to glass.
49.meet: The transparent conductor in touchscreens (indium tin oxide).

50.hook: Bends with a crackling “tin cry”, and crumbles to powder in severe cold.

51.hook: A brittle metalloid ancient Egyptians ground into eyeliner.

52.hook: Rarer than gold in Earth’s crust.

53.hook: A dark solid that turns straight into violet vapour when warmed.
53.meet: Iodised salt, antiseptics, your thyroid hormones.

54.hook: The first noble gas shown to form compounds.
54.meet: Bright car headlights, ion engines on spacecraft, anaesthesia.

55.hook: One of the most reactive metals, and the one that defines the second.

56.hook: Heavy and toxic, yet its sulfate is safe to swallow because it does not dissolve.
56.meet: Barium meals for X-rays, green fireworks.

58.hook: The most abundant rare-earth metal; it throws sparks when scraped.
58.meet: Lighter flints, catalytic converters, glass polishing.

59.hook: Tints glass and ceramics a bright yellow-green.
59.meet: Welders’ goggles, strong magnets, aircraft-engine alloys.

60.hook: Makes the strongest permanent magnets there are.

61.hook: A rare earth with no stable isotope; nearly all of it is made in reactors.

62.hook: Samarium–cobalt magnets keep their strength when hot.

63.hook: Glows red or blue under UV light, which helps prove euro banknotes are real.
63.meet: Phosphors in screens and LEDs, anti-forgery inks.

64.hook: Magnetic only below about 20 °C, and it absorbs neutrons extremely well.
64.meet: MRI contrast agents, reactor safety systems.

65.hook: Makes a bright green glow, and its alloys change shape in a magnetic field.
65.meet: Green phosphors, sonar and precision actuators.

66.hook: Keeps neodymium magnets strong when they heat up.

67.hook: Has the largest magnetic moment of any naturally occurring element.
67.meet: Pole pieces of the strongest electromagnets, surgical lasers.

68.hook: Amplifies the light signals that carry the internet under the oceans.
68.meet: Fibre-optic amplifiers, pink glass, laser skin treatment.

70.hook: Powers some of the most precise atomic clocks ever built.

72.hook: Zirconium’s chemical twin, except that it gobbles neutrons instead of letting them through.
72.meet: Reactor control rods, the insulating layers in modern chips.

73.hook: Almost immune to corrosion, even inside the human body.

74.hook: Has the highest melting point of any metal: 3,422 °C.
74.meet: Old light-bulb filaments, drill bits, heavy alloys.

75.hook: The last stable element discovered, and one of the rarest.

76.hook: The densest natural element: a fist-sized lump weighs about as much as a bowling ball.

77.hook: The most corrosion-resistant metal, and a clue to what ended the dinosaurs.
77.meet: Spark plugs, crucibles, the old standard kilogram.

78.hook: A precious metal that is also a superb catalyst.
78.meet: Catalytic converters, jewellery, the cancer drug cisplatin.

79.hook: So unreactive it stays shiny for thousands of years; a gram can be beaten into a sheet about a square metre wide.

80.hook: The only metal that is liquid at room temperature.
80.meet: Old thermometers, fluorescent lamps, dental amalgam.

82.hook: Dense, soft and easy to melt; used since Roman times, now restricted as a poison.

83.hook: Technically radioactive, but with a half-life over a billion times the age of the universe.
83.meet: Pink stomach remedies, lead-free solder, rainbow-coloured crystals.

84.hook: Intensely radioactive: a gram heats itself to about 500 °C.
84.meet: Anti-static brushes for camera lenses and film.

85.hook: The rarest naturally occurring element: under a gram in Earth’s crust at any moment.

86.hook: A radioactive gas that seeps out of rocks into basements.

87.hook: So unstable that no visible lump of it has ever existed.

88.hook: Glows faintly blue; Marie and Pierre Curie discovered it.
88.meet: Old luminous watch dials, cancer treatment (radium-223).

89.hook: Glows pale blue in the dark from its own radioactivity.

90.hook: About three times as abundant as uranium, and a possible nuclear fuel.

91.hook: One of the rarest and most toxic natural elements.

92.hook: The heaviest element found in quantity in nature; its slow decay helps heat Earth’s interior.

93.hook: The first element heavier than uranium, made in 1940.

94.hook: Made by the tonne in reactors; one isotope powers deep-space probes.
94.meet: Nuclear weapons and fuel, the power sources of Voyager and Curiosity.

95.hook: The only synthetic element in many homes.

96.hook: So radioactive it glows; it powered instruments on Mars rovers.
96.meet: Alpha sources in rover X-ray spectrometers.

97.hook: Made only in a couple of reactors, in milligram amounts.
97.meet: Target material for making heavier elements.

98.hook: A fierce neutron source: one microgram gives off over two million neutrons a second.
98.meet: Starting up reactors, finding oil and gold deposits.

99.hook: First found in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb.
99.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.

100.hook: The heaviest element that can be built by adding neutrons one at a time.
100.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.

101.hook: The first element made and detected one atom at a time.
101.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.

102.hook: Its discovery was disputed between laboratories in three countries for years.
102.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.

103.hook: Named after Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron.
103.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.

104.hook: The first element past the actinides; its name was fought over in the “Transfermium Wars”.
104.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.

105.hook: Named after Dubna, the Russian town of the laboratory that helped make it.
105.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.

106.hook: The first element named after a living person, Glenn Seaborg.
106.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.

107.hook: Made by fusing chromium with bismuth, one atom at a time.
107.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.

108.hook: Predicted to be one of the densest substances of all, if enough could ever be made.
108.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.

109.hook: Named for Lise Meitner, who helped explain nuclear fission.
109.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.

110.hook: Its longest-lived known isotopes last only seconds.
110.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.

111.hook: Expected to be a heavy cousin of gold.
111.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.

112.hook: Relativity may make it behave almost like a noble gas.
112.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.

113.hook: The first element discovered in Asia.
113.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.

114.hook: Sits near a predicted “island of stability” of longer-lived superheavy nuclei.
114.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.

115.hook: Its decay chain gave the first atoms of element 113 made in Russia.
115.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.

116.hook: Its atoms survive for only milliseconds.
116.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.

117.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.

118.hook: The heaviest element known; theory suggests it may not even behave like a gas.
118.meet: Only in research labs, a few atoms at a time.
